text:
Rose, totally agree. 

Long post! Thx in advance for reading.

Homelessness is complex. 

I volunteered for a short time with a Christian urban ministry in CA. Dont want to give its name, ‘cause I dont speak for it. It is a faith-based organization. 

I don’t always know what my beliefs are, but their beliefs are v clear. Jesus walks with these people. ❤️

I went with the Ministry to Mississippi after Hurricane Katrina wrecked the Gulf coast. 

The Ministry went to Biloxi to hand out food and water and help the people recover. While I was there I met one of the Ministry’s homeless program’s “graduates,” Kraig. 

Kraig was a heroin addict for many years, living on the street in towns up and down the west coast. 

He ended up going to prison in Nevada. Told me he got sober and found Christ in prison, and connected with the Ministry when he got out. 

The info below is the process the Ministry uses to help homelessness. 

The process is extensive, but it’s probably what’s actually required to take a homeless person off the streets and get them into a permanently “stable” life. 

I challenge anyone to look at the process and see if any city in the US could provide this level of primary, continuing aid. 

Kraig said the average time in the Ministry of moving from homelessness to “permanent stability” was greater than two years.

Their process, as I understood it:

The Ministry takes a homeless man off of the street, and initially offers: 

A bed in a night shelter
A chance to shower, shave 
A change of clothes
A meal 
Immediate urgent medical care 
A 12-step meeting

The requirement: the man must follow rules in the shelter, including no drugs, drinking, violence or aggression.

Man is evaluated. If the man is willing, and accepted, he enters the long-term program. In the program, man is given: 

a shared long-term room
regular meals
access to shower 
hygiene supplies
new clothes
continuing urgent medical care
access to 12-step programs

The man is expected to follow the rules, attend faith-based services and classes, interact with a 12-step program, and contribute to the Ministry’s programs (e.g. prepare meals, counsel new members, clean the shelter, follow through on commitments.) No drugs or alcohol are allowed. No uncivil behavior. The man is held accountable. 

In return, the Ministry will also help the man:

get a legal ID 
find permanent housing 
reconnect with his family, if desired
complete a high school GED 
obtain a driver’s license 
receive long-term counseling 
continue in 12-step programs
find a job (the Ministry created a whole job center just for these men; they often work together in construction teams; make good money.) 
find education or training 
receive bilingual language training if needed

The Ministry has an equivalent program for women. 

The Ministry has an equivalent program for parents with minor children.

I don’t know the Ministry’s statistics - don’t know how many people enter the programs, how many “graduate”, how many go on to achieve long-term stability. I think the numbers are probably pretty good. I can’t imagine the costs involved. I believe the Ministry is nonprofit. 

Kraig entered the program as a homeless, recovering addict and felon. When I met him in Mississippi, he was training to become a Christian minister, was working full time in a good construction job, and was helping a mostly-black Christian  congregation in Biloxi put a new roof on their church. Kraig is a white man. Kraig is a good man. 

Homelessness is complex. It can be solved, but it requires long-term commitment and continuing investment over years in many areas of a person’s life. 

This is the kind of investment a family  makes in their members.

The Ministry is stepping into people’s lives and caring for them like family.

I think it’s very challenging for any city to try to take this on, even if given millions of dollars. 

In LA county, CA, alone, the estimate of homeless addicted people is something like 30,000.

Tulane Green Wave

Class of 2026 Spotlight

DE
 Jordyn Crites- @JordynCrites26 
6-7/274
Friendswood, TX
 Jordyn Crites is a towering defensive lineman from Friendswood High School in Friendswood, Texas, class of 2026. 
 Standing at 6-7 and weighing 274 pounds, Crites combines exceptional length with athleticism, making him a disruptive force on the edge or interior. 
 He signed with Tulane on December 3, 2025, after committing on June 14, 2025, choosing the Green Wave over 16 FBS offers, including Power 4 programs like Baylor, TCU, Oregon State, Texas Tech, and others such as Coastal Carolina, Louisiana, North Texas, Rice, San Diego State, Tulsa, UNLV, and UTEP.     
 Crites transferred to Friendswood after attending Edmond Memorial in Oklahoma for his freshman and sophomore years, where he began building his profile.   
 He also played tight end, showcasing versatility, but his future is on defense. 
 Crites was noted as a “riser” in recruiting circles.   
 His recruitment heated up with official visits to TCU, Tulane, and Baylor in June 2025.  Crites was praised for his potential as one of the top defensive linemen from Texas, with Power 4 interest. 
 Scouting Report:
 Frame and Length: 
Enormous wingspan and height make him a mismatch nightmare, allowing him to disrupt passing lanes and engulf ball carriers. His reach helps in shedding blocks and maintaining leverage.   
 Power and Hand Usage: 
Violent, heavy hands at the point of attack; primary move is a pure power rush that overwhelms offensive linemen. He can swim and dodge as counters, showing developing technique. 
 Athleticism and Bend: 
Exceptional bend for his size, allowing him to break down in the backfield and pursue with speed. His 4.8 40 and vertical translate to explosive get-off and closing burst. 
 Motor and Production: 
High-motor player who lives in the backfield, generating sacks, hurries, and numerous tackles for loss (TFLs). Effective against both run and pass, with a dynamic presence that wrecks games. 
 Versatility and Upside: 
Two-way experience (DE/TE), with unreal potential due to size, power, and athleticism. He’s come into his own recently, suggesting continued growth. 
 Intangibles: 
Strong academics, track background, and resilience shown in transferring schools.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Shawn Ryan Show: #334 Clint Emerson - Inside SEAL Team 6's Spy Unit: Black Squadron

Overview

Clint Emerson's path from an American childhood inside Saudi Arabia to the silent ranks of SEAL Team 6 is a study in the formation of a special operator. His early exposure to a strict, sometimes hostile, foreign culture instilled a specific drive, but it was a near-drowning as a child that became his psychological anchor for surviving the brutal crucible of BUD/S. This conversation spans the absurdity and danger of pre-9/11 SEAL life, from hazing rituals and training with killer dolphins to the grim, chaotic opening months of the Iraq War. The threads that bind these experiences are the unspoken codes of brotherhood, the persistent tension between enlisted operators and risk-averse leadership, and a deep-seated need to prove one's worth that never fully extinguishes, even after reaching the pinnacle of the special operations community. Emerson’s story is not just about combat; it is about the personal cost, dark humor, and profound trauma that forge a warrior’s identity.

Key Themes

- Childhood adversity, specifically a near-fatal scuba diving scare, becomes a deliberate psychological tool used to reframe the suffering of SEAL training as manageable.
- A lifetime of low-level hostility and cultural alienation in Saudi Arabia directly fueled Emerson's motivation to enlist and later deploy to the Middle East with a desire for retribution.
- An unyielding code of silence among operators is paramount; Emerson endured severe physical punishment rather than identify an instructor who caused a classmate's career-ending injury.
- The pre-9/11 SEAL teams were a paradox, operating with less tactical intensity but engaging in dangerous hazing and serving as training apparatuses for military dolphins.
- A perpetual conflict exists between enlisted men who seek to execute their mission and senior officers whose lack of combat experience and risk aversion hamstrings their effectiveness.
- Combat in the early Iraq War was characterized by chaos, unclear lines of engagement, and a stark contrast between the grimy reality of the line units and the well-equipped, surgical operations of higher-tier commands.
- The trauma of a broken home and the pressure of an uncelebrated stepfather drive a persistent need to prove one's worth that extends far beyond earning a Trident.

Detailed Summary

Emerson began his life in Texas before his father's work for ARAMCO relocated the family to Abqaiq, Saudi Arabia. He spent his formative years on a secure Western compound, an environment punctuated by anti-aircraft guns and razor wire. The Kingdom in the 1980s, as he recalls, was a radical Islamic state with a rigid social hierarchy. Westerners were second-class citizens, forced to yield at every queue and subject to harassment, with young Saudi men throwing hard leather sandals at him from distances that felt like being hit by a plate. The system was flush with oil money but morally contradictory; Coca-Cola was banned due to its purported Crusader symbolism, while visas required costly annual exits from the country.

The strict environment defined his worldview. He left the region because schools only went to eighth grade. The turning point came in a Frankfurt airport, where a chance encounter with a Navy SEAL—recounting a mission to neutralize anti-aircraft guns before a bombing run—changed his ambition from ninja to frogman. This was reinforced by a school aptitude test that matched him with underwater demolition. The final nudge was a literal life-or-death experience. At twelve, on his first open-water dive at Tire Reef in the Persian Gulf, he became separated from his group and panicked. After what felt like a lifetime of treading water, he kicked hard enough to spot land and swam back, an experience that later served as a touchstone: "I've already been lost at sea." BUD/S, he reasoned, could not be worse.

This psychological anchor proved vital. Emerson enlisted in the Navy despite being close to a college degree, hiding his decision until two weeks before boot camp. At BUD/S, as a student named Smith in Class 203, he was repeatedly blamed for the deficiencies of other Smiths, accumulating punishment chits and extra sessions with a "wired tight" instructor fresh from SEAL Team 6. During one session, the instructor kicked another trainee, Garcia, breaking his ankle. While the class pressured Emerson to name the instructor, he refused, enduring a "death march" and continuous beatings rather than violate the code. Years later, he ran into the same man, now a warrant officer, and revealed he had saved his career. The man admitted he had "almost got cam" for the incident, and they shared a laugh, a moment of closure for both.

His determination was rooted in a desire to return to Saudi Arabia and "mess with these people." He also sought to prove he was not a loser, a feeling born from his pre-Navy life. This drive to prove his worth persisted even after making it to a tier-one command. The conversation noted the common lore that most special operators come from broken homes; Emerson speculated that his own childhood trauma was a beacon for what could be overcome. The loss of his stepfather, who died suddenly of a heart attack right as he was finishing training at SEAL Team 3, added another layer of grief and motivation. His stepfather had volunteered to raise him, and Emerson wanted to share his SEAL stories with the man who truly earned them. This emotional weight was something he learned to compartmentalize, to "deep six it" and deal with it later.

Life at SEAL Team 3 pre-9/11 was its own distinct world. The culture was less intense than today's, characterized by liberty and hazing rituals that could turn dangerous. Emerson recounted his own "initiation," involving being stripped and taped with blasting machine leads attached, nearly thrown into a covered pool. Training was often ad-hoc. In one memorable exercise, his platoon chief, a former Marine, bear-hugged a pier pylon while Emerson lay on the sandy bottom, both using Draeger rebreathers to avoid Navy dolphins. These dolphins, equipped with harnesses and capable of killing a great white shark, "took turns punching" the chief. The primary job was to serve as training apparatus, with the famous dolphin Jake rumored to have broken several operators' bones before being retired and deployed to harbors worldwide.

The pre-9/11 operational focus was ship boarding in the Persian Gulf. Team 3 had become "the pros," inventing protocols to infiltrate behind tankers using radar shadows and scaling six-inch-wide caving ladders at 20 knots in rough seas to board vessels and hand them over to NATO forces. It was one of the few operational jobs available, making it a sought-after deployment. The world changed on 9/11, which Emerson watched unfold from the Team 3 quarterdeck after receiving a phone call while driving across the Coronado Bridge. The pace shifted from "ops of the decade" to "ops of the night." On the way into Iraq, morale was complicated. At a staging base in Kuwait, they built a "tent city" with mocking signs aimed at reserve officers seeking combat experience, which leadership tolerated to keep spirits up, followed by a "war garden."

The first major operation was a gas-oil platform, which the command decided to approach by loud jetboat rather than stealth. The intel suggested a handful of bad guys and a hostage, but they found dozens. The platform was 1 kilometer long, seven decks high, and wired to explode. The assault was chaotic, with a nervous boat crewman accidentally firing the first shot into an oil pipe. They cleared the structure, finding shoulder-fired weapons and explosives below the waterline, and ultimately killed 27 enemy fighters. Afterward, they drove north in unarmored Humvees into a war that defied expectations. They witnessed the grim reality of trench warfare and slept on medical waste covered in hypodermic needles. The team was ordered by Colonel Kelly, later General Kelly, to conduct "100 killer ops" against a city of 80,000 with just 16 men.

Their missions were often dark and covert. At night, they secretly pulled the bodies of dead Marines from front-line trenches to protect morale, attributing the deaths to "fedeyeen" throat-cutters, a rumor that gave Emerson nightmares. They engaged in hunter-killer missions against Scud sites and cleared buildings ahead of the line. The conflict was starkly different from the sanitized public perception, as they saw burned-out US tanks and convoys. At one point, the entire convoy fell asleep at sunrise near "Toree," forcing Emerson to wake dozens of vehicles to avoid being sitting ducks. From a distance, he witnessed the Jessica Lynch rescue, contrasting his grimy reality with the "Guccied out" SEAL Team Six operators who annihilated the target from their armored supercharged Humvees.

These experiences highlighted the tension between enlisted operators and their leadership. Emerson openly challenged Captain Harwood in a debrief, accusing him of hamstringing the team and preventing them from doing what they were trained to do. He saw the early war's ROE as dangerously ambiguous, where every male of fighting age was a potential threat. Despite being offered a path to become an officer, he threw the OCS package in the trash in front of his chief, choosing to remain enlisted, where he felt the true operators "ran the show." The enduring impression is that the spirit of the SEAL teams is carried by its enlisted men, who navigate the absurdity and trauma of war with a dark humor and a fierce, unbreakable loyalty to each other.

Avatar: The Last Airbender: The Official Book of Amigurumi is an official standalone crochet pattern book published by Insight Editions. This original collection expands the world of the animated series into the realm of crafting, taking makers on a deeper journey through the beloved characters and creatures of the Four Nations.

The craft book features more than 20 standalone crochet projects, bringing together iconic heroes, villains, spirits, and creatures through a shared celebration of creativity. Rather than following a single narrative arc, the collection offers handmade interpretations of characters from the beloved series, including members of Team Avatar, Uncle Iroh, and the Cabbage Merchant, alongside memorable creatures such as Appa and the Turtle Ducks.

The 144-page book is written by Lee Sartori who created most of the designs. Guest pattern designs include @chrisette_ , who designed the Turtle Duck and Monk Gyatso, and cozylittlemess on IG, who designed June and Nyla as part of the QR bonus content. The collaborative project also features full-color photography, clear step-by-step instructions, and essential stitch tutorials.

The collection brings the world of Avatar: The Last Airbender beyond the screen, allowing fans to crochet their way through the Four Nations. With projects ranging from beginner-friendly creations to more intermediate designs, the book offers makers the opportunity to bring their favorite benders, characters, and companion creatures to life.

Official News Release:
Junction City Council confirms employment offer to Benjamin West
08/27/26

The City Council for Junction City confirmed an employment offer to Ben West of Wilsonville, OR, to serve as Junction City’s next City Administrator. The Council also authorized the Mayor and Council President to negotiate an employment agreement with West for later adoption by the Council. The City Council made the initial offer on August 18, following a two-day interview process subject to completion of the background check. Council reviewed criminal history, civil litigation, verification of employment and education, and reference checks to address this matter.

One issue the Council reviewed in detail was an ethics complaint filed in May regarding Clackamas County's employment of Ben West’s father in a temporary position. By all accounts, Mr. West’s involvement leading to the complaint was an inquiry he made to the County Administrator about whether there were any job openings relating to his father’s skill set. There is no evidence that he had any further involvement in securing a job for his father. Mr. West attended an executive session to directly answer any questions the Council had about his background, specifically the ethics complaint. In consultation with Junction City’s legal counsel and the City Administrator Pro Tem, Council agreed that the nature of this complaint would not have an impact on his suitability to fill this position.

Mayor Ken Wells stated: “It is important for the Council to do due diligence to understand the background of Mr. West to ensure that he would be a good fit to fill the position of City Administrator. Following this review, the Council was comfortable with proceeding with negotiating an employment agreement with Ben.”

“I am genuinely eager to serve as the next City Administrator for Junction City and to become an integral part of this community,” stated West. “My enthusiasm runs deep, and I am confident we will work effectively together to address Junction City’s pressing issues.”

West is completing a four-year term as a County Commissioner in Clackamas County (pop. 421,000) and is a US Navy Reserve Lieutenant and Registered Nurse. Ben also served as City Councilor for Wilsonville from 2019 to 2022.

West has taken the lead role in working through a variety of hurdles that led to a $44 million Recovery Campus and transitional housing project for Clackamas County, which had groundbreaking ceremonies. He has worked closely with many officials and agencies in Oregon on various funding and policy issues for Clackamas County. In the Navy Reserves, he serves as a commissioned officer in a complex, mission-driven organization.

For further information, contact:
Spencer Nebel, City Administrator Pro Tem, snebel@ci.junction-city.or.us
Phone (541) 998-2153

text:
🏈 NOTRE DAME + G5

• Year two of CJ Carr. He already owns Notre Dame's passing efficiency record, and the offense now runs through him after losing the first two RBs drafted.
• Carr's next leap: pre-snap reads, pocket strength and playing calmer. His worst games came vs. USC, Texas A&M and Miami.
• Defense could be elite: four veteran CBs, two top recruits, both safeties back, full LB rotation and Oregon transfer T'Vondre Gray inside. 11-1 is the expectation.

🏈 G5
BOISE STATE
• The new Pac-12 has real depth — no easy weeks. Boise can't afford any sleepwalk games.
• Maddux Madsen's growth comes from tougher opponents. His struggles have come against Penn State, Notre Dame, USF and Washington.
• RB room may be the best in the G5. 10-2 likely gets playoff consideration; 9-3 probably misses.

FRESNO STATE
• Fresno ranked THIRD nationally in returning production from the portal. Players chose to stay despite bigger offers.
• Brian Ferentz takes over OL, and getting Roland Follywood back at RT solves a major roster concern.
• QB remains the biggest question. After last year's carousel, the cornerback room will decide the ceiling.

USF
• Brian Hartline brings a complete culture shift: CEO-style leadership after Golesh's offensive identity.
• Tim Beck installs a slower pro-style offense — the biggest question is whether it fits USF's tempo-driven success.
• Defense replaces nearly every star with transfers. Floor is around 7-5; ceiling is winning the American.

This goes back to the capture of science by Pharma, & of government by the corporate sector generally - including Pharma.

This has got little to do with objective science. I did a deep dive on this in a new book (1,600 citations).

Here's how ‘The Science’ is arrived at:

- 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝗶𝗱 𝗯𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘃𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗲-𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗿 (𝗻𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆).

(The few independent trials have a much lower success rate than the Pharma-funded ones. And they identify many times the side effects.)

- 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗹𝘀’ '𝗮𝗿𝗺𝘀𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵' ‘𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁’ 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗲𝘀 (𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗰𝘀, 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗲𝘁𝗰) 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝘆𝗽𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗽𝗮𝗶𝗱 𝗯𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗲-𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗼𝗼.

- 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗽𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝗷𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘀 𝗸𝗲𝗽𝘁 𝗮𝗳𝗹𝗼𝗮𝘁 𝗯𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘃𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗲-𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗿 & 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗿𝘂𝗴 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗲𝘀, 𝘃𝗶𝗮𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴.

- 𝗔𝗱𝗱𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗷𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘀’ 𝗲𝗱𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀, 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗱𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆, 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝗶𝗱 ‘𝗳𝗲𝗲𝘀’ 𝗯𝘆 𝗣𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗺𝗮.

(In 2014, each editor of 𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘈𝘮𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘯 𝘊𝘰𝘭𝘭𝘦𝘨𝘦 𝘰𝘧 𝘊𝘢𝘳𝘥𝘪𝘰𝘭𝘰𝘨𝘺  received, on average, $475,072. Plus another $119,407 for ‘research’.)

Most stages in the lab-to-jab pipeline have this double layer of 'insurance'.

- 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘃𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝘆 𝗮 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗿𝗲𝗴𝘂𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆. 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗣𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗺𝗮, 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺 𝗼𝗳 𝗳𝗲𝗲𝘀.

(E.g. Australia’s Therapeutic Goods Administration gets 96% of its funding from the drug & vaccine industry.)

- 𝗦𝗼 𝗱𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗴𝘂𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀’ ‘𝗮𝗿𝗺𝘀𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵’, ‘𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁’ 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗲𝘀. 𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲, 𝗕𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗻’𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗴𝘂𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗵𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰 𝗠𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘁 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗽, ‘𝗮𝗻 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗲’ 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗲𝘀 ‘𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲’ 𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝘃𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀. 𝗜𝘁𝘀 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗰𝗲𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆.

- 𝗜𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗿𝗲𝗴𝘂𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲 '𝘄𝗶𝘀𝗲𝗹𝘆', 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝗱𝗼 𝘄𝗲𝗹𝗹—𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺 𝗼𝗳 𝗴𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝗣𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗺𝗮 𝗷𝗼𝗯𝘀𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝘃𝗲.

- 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗱𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀—& 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗴𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻 𝘃𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗿𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘂𝘁—𝘁𝘆𝗽𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗲𝗻𝗷𝗼𝘆 𝗹𝗮𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗰𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗯𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗣𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗺𝗮, & 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘁𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗱𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽𝘀 & 𝗽𝗮𝗶𝗱 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀.

“𝑻𝒉𝒆 𝒄𝒐𝒏𝒕𝒓𝒂𝒄𝒕 𝒉𝒂𝒔 𝒃𝒆𝒆𝒏 𝒈𝒊𝒗𝒆𝒏 𝒃𝒚 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝑴𝑯𝑹𝑨 [𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒓𝒆𝒈𝒖𝒍𝒂𝒕𝒐𝒓]—𝒘𝒉𝒐 𝒂𝒓𝒆 86% 𝒇𝒖𝒏𝒅𝒆𝒅 𝒕𝒉𝒆𝒎𝒔𝒆𝒍𝒗𝒆𝒔 𝒃𝒚 𝑩𝒊𝒈𝑷𝒉𝒂𝒓𝒎𝒂—𝒕𝒐 𝒂 𝒄𝒐𝒎𝒑𝒂𝒏𝒚 𝒘𝒉𝒊𝒄𝒉 𝒊𝒔 𝒇𝒖𝒏𝒅𝒆𝒅 𝒃𝒚 𝑩𝒊𝒈 𝑷𝒉𝒂𝒓𝒎𝒂, 𝒕𝒐 𝒊𝒏𝒗𝒆𝒔𝒕𝒊𝒈𝒂𝒕𝒆 𝒄𝒐𝒎𝒑𝒍𝒂𝒊𝒏𝒕𝒔 𝒂𝒈𝒂𝒊𝒏𝒔𝒕 𝑩𝒊𝒈𝑷𝒉𝒂𝒓𝒎𝒂.”

In the book* I dub the impact of this long list of paid ‘voices’ 'the chorus effect'. The objective is 'end-to-end narrative containment'.

Most of the pipeline’s stages are shrouded in sepulchral secrecy. For example:

· 𝗪𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗸𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗣𝗳𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗿 𝗺𝗮𝗱𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗽𝘂𝘁 𝘂𝗽 𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗯𝗮𝗻𝗸 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝘀, 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀 & 𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗮𝘀𝘀𝘆 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝘁 𝗮𝗴𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝗶𝗺𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘃𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗲𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀.

· 𝗜𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗮 𝗹𝗮𝘄𝘀𝘂𝗶𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝗲𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗣𝗳𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗿 𝘃𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗙𝗗𝗔 𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗮 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲—𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘀𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵—𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝟮𝟬𝟵𝟳. (𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗳𝘀 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗱, 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗻 ‘𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗳 𝗼𝗹𝗱 𝗮𝗴𝗲’.)

The vaccine industry lives or dies by the chorus effect.

Its messages reach the public ear from a wide array of sources—expected & unexpected, central & marginal, official & unofficial—to create an impression of broad, & very diverse, support.

The 'chorus' is hired via a financial inducement to every player in the system—& even at its edges—from the one party with an overwhelming commercial interest in the outcome.

"𝑰 𝒅𝒐, 𝒚𝒆𝒔—𝒊𝒕'𝒔 𝒕𝒆𝒏 𝒕𝒉𝒐𝒖𝒔𝒂𝒏𝒅 𝒔𝒕𝒆𝒓𝒍𝒊𝒏𝒈."

— 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝘁 𝗛𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗰𝗸, 𝗕𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘀𝗵 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗵 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝗿𝗲𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗮𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗢𝗩𝗜𝗗 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲—𝗼𝗻 𝗯𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝘀𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗳 𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗮𝗱 𝗮 𝗱𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘆𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗻 𝗮 𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗽𝗼𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗯𝗼𝗮𝗿𝗱.

Pharma can wait out RFK’s term—then pay off Congress to roll back his reforms.

Which means we need permanent political architecture to prevent this kind of system capture.

Or, longterm: more of the same.

"NO ONE KNOWS HOW LONG THE SHORTAGE WILL LAST" - FULL $SKHY CEO INTERVIEW

SK Hynix CEO Kwak No-jung predicted that the memory semiconductor supply shortage will continue until the end of 2030, and that there will not be a sharp decline in demand thereafter.

Regarding plans for additional investment in the U.S., he reaffirmed the existing stance that investment is possible anywhere sufficient support is provided.

CEO Kwak gave this response to a question regarding how long he expects the memory supply shortage to continue during a press conference following the groundbreaking ceremony for an advanced packaging production base for AI memory at Purdue University’s Holloway Gymnasium in West Lafayette, Indiana, on the 27th (local time).

"No one knows how long the shortage will last, but there are no clear signs of a downturn," said CEO Kwak. "We expect the shortage to continue until the end of 2030."

He further explained, "I believe the next downturn will be different from the ones we have experienced over the past few decades. While adjusting production volumes appropriately is not easy, our business model for AI is transitioning from 100% standard products to partially customized or fully customized products."

In the case of AI memory, since it is custom-made for client systems, demand forecasting is easier and ties with manufacturers are stronger compared to the past. Consequently, the explanation is that even if a downturn occurs, the damage will not be as severe as in the past."

Even if a downturn hits, I believe demand will slow down slightly or remain at a stable level rather than plummeting," CEO Kwak said. "Therefore, I am not concerned about the period after 2030. I believe supply and demand will balance out, and the entire AI industry will grow together."

When asked about plans to invest in additional semiconductor production facilities in the U.S., he replied, "We are open to any location where sufficient resources, such as water, electricity, talent, and subsidies, are provided," adding, "Since nothing has been finalized yet, I cannot discuss specific details or directions."

Last month, SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won stated, "If there is a suitable place, it does not matter whether it is the United States or anywhere in the world," expressing the same position.

However, CEO Kwak specifically added, "I hope to be able to deliver good news to the U.S. AI industry next time."

When asked if he felt pressured by the Donald Trump administration's demand for investment in memory semiconductor front-end process facilities, he replied, "Our current situation is very well known through media reports."

He reiterated, "We are reviewing any location in the world as long as it offers customers and new business opportunities," adding, "If the conditions presented by the other party are met, we would like to deliver another piece of good news to the AI industry in the U.S. or other countries, just like at today's event."

Regarding whether to continue maintaining its stake in the Japanese NAND flash company Kioxia (formerly Toshiba Memory), he answered, "There are no concrete or confirmed plans yet."

He further explained, "However, just as we contribute to the U.S. AI industry, we also intend to contribute to the Japanese semiconductor industry. Since we are investing in Japan just as we have in the U.S., we view it as our responsibility in some respects to contribute to that local community and the nation. Although there are no confirmed plans, we are carefully examining how we can grow the market together."
